Dataset choice is a model choice. The object vocabulary, the image source, the annotation policy, and the class frequencies define what “good detection” means. Benchmark scores do not transfer automatically: audit domain shift, missing labels (Open Images and LVIS are federated — not every image is exhaustively labelled for every class), duplicated categories, and deployment costs.


13.2 Running a pretrained detector
import torch
from torchvision.io import read_image
from torchvision.models.detection import (
    fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn, FasterRCNN_ResNet50_FPN_Weights,
)

weights = FasterRCNN_ResNet50_FPN_Weights.DEFAULT
model = fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn(weights=weights, box_score_thresh=0.5).eval()
preprocess = weights.transforms()                  # the checkpoint's own preprocessing

image = read_image("street.png")[:3]               # (3, H, W), uint8
with torch.no_grad():
    out = model([preprocess(image)])[0]            # dict: boxes, labels, scores

names = [weights.meta["categories"][i] for i in out["labels"]]
The model takes a list of images of any size, resizes them internally, and returns boxes in the original image’s pixel coordinates, already post-processed by NMS. box_score_thresh is an inference-time choice — evaluate with a low threshold, deploy with the one your application needs.


13.3 Failure modes







Figure 51: Diagnose, don’t guess: a poorly fitted box, a wrong class, and a duplicate on the scene.





Classification: wrong label, or background hallucinated as an object.
Localization: a shifted or oversized box — counted as a TP at IoU \(0.5\) but as an FP at \(0.75\).
Coverage: small or occluded objects missed.
Multiplicity: duplicates, or two adjacent instances merged into one box.
Shift: sensor, weather, and geography differ between training and deployment.

Slice errors by class, scale, occlusion, and domain. One mAP number hides the cause.

Check 5 — Boxes are coarse; pixels matter







Figure 52: Left, detection: boxes include background and erase shape. Right, dense prediction: masks preserve boundaries, shape, and contact.




A box around the cyclist contains as much road as cyclist. For a robot grasping an object, a car estimating free space, or a radiologist measuring a tumour, that is not good enough. The next part predicts a label — or an instance identity — for every pixel (He et al. 2017).

Part IVSegmentation

title: From pixels to structured scene understanding
text:
14 Semantic segmentation







Figure 53: Semantic segmentation assigns one class to every pixel: building, road, sidewalk.




A semantic segmentation network outputs a score for every class at every pixel and takes the most likely one:
\[
\mathbf{z}=f_\theta(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C},
\qquad
\hat y_{ij}=\arg\max_{c}\,z_{ijc}.
\tag{17}\]
The output remains aligned with the input image. Amorphous “stuff” (road, sky, vegetation) and countable “things” (car, person) share one label map, and same-class objects are not separated into instances: two adjacent pedestrians become one “person” region. Classification asks what; segmentation asks what at each location.







Figure 54: The same scene as a detection output — a set \(\{(c_k,s_k,\mathbf{b}_k)\}_{k=1}^{K}\) — and as a segmentation output — a map \(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}\in\{1,\dots,C\}^{H\times W}\).







Table 8: Detection and semantic segmentation answer different questions.






Detection
Semantic segmentation




Geometry
coarse box extent
object boundaries and background


Identity
separates detections
merges pixels of the same class


Supervision
boxes
pixel-level masks






Pixel-level masks are expensive: a COCO-style polygon takes minutes per object, against seconds for a box. That cost is a recurring theme of the course, and one reason why promptable segmentation foundation models such as SAM (Kirillov et al. 2023) matter.

14.1 Naive patch classification







Figure 55: Classify the centre pixel of a crop, for every pixel. Neighbouring patches overlap almost completely.




The first idea is to train a classifier on a crop around each pixel and predict that pixel’s label (Farabet et al. 2013). It is correct but wasteful: neighbouring patches overlap almost completely, so their convolutional features are recomputed again and again; small patches miss context while large ones multiply the cost; and a full image needs about \(H\times W\) classifier calls — 330 000 for a \(432\times768\) image. Exactly as for detection, the missing ingredient is shared computation.


14.2 Fully convolutional networks







Figure 56: A fully convolutional network on the scene (torchvision’s FCN-ResNet50). Shared convolutions turn a \(432\times768\times3\) image into a \(54\times96\times2048\) map, computed once — one vector per \(8\times8\)-pixel region; a \(1\times1\) convolution gives \(21\) class scores per cell; bilinear upsampling \(\times8\) returns to full resolution; the arg max over classes gives the label map.




The fully convolutional network (Long et al. 2015) makes the same conversion as Figure 38: replace the classifier’s dense layers by convolutions, and spatial score maps emerge in one forward pass. The resulting network

accepts variable image sizes, since nothing in it depends on \(H\) or \(W\);
shares features across locations;
trades resolution for receptive field — its coarse output must be upsampled.

Dense prediction does not require dense repetition. What it does require is a way to recover the resolution lost in the encoder.


14.3 Encoder–decoder design







Figure 57: The encoder (real ResNet-50 activations on the scene) reduces \(432\times768\) to \(14\times24\) at stride 32 while increasing channels from 256 to 2048; the decoder (here an FCN’s prediction shown at each resolution) upsamples back through strides 16, 8, and 4 to the full-resolution mask.




The encoder answers what?: downsampling enlarges the receptive field and builds invariance, but discards precise location. The decoder answers where?: upsampling restores spatial resolution, but must reconstruct boundaries from compressed features. Segmentation needs both global context and pixel-level localization, and every architecture below is a different compromise between them.


14.4 Upsampling methods







Figure 58: Four ways to upsample a real \(8\times8\) patch of FCN “car” scores at the car’s edge to \(16\times16\). Nearest copies each value \(2\times2\) (blocky, no parameters); bilinear takes a weighted average of neighbours (smooth); a transposed convolution with kernel 3 and stride 2 has a learned kernel but uneven overlap — each output pixel receives 1, 2, or 4 inputs, the source of checkerboard artefacts; resize then \(3\times3\) convolution is a robust default.




A transposed convolution (“deconvolution”, although it inverts nothing) is the adjoint of a strided convolution: each input value scatters a scaled copy of the kernel into the output, with a step of \(S\) (Dumoulin and Visin 2016). Its output size is
\[
H'=(H-1)S-2P+D(K-1)+P_{\text{out}}+1,
\]
so \(K=3\), \(S=2\), \(P=1\), \(P_{\text{out}}=1\) maps \(8\to16\). When \(K\) is not divisible by \(S\), the scattered kernels overlap unevenly: in 1-D with \(K=3\), \(S=2\), even outputs receive two contributions and odd outputs one; in 2-D the counts are \(1\), \(2\), and \(4\), a periodic pattern that the learned weights must fight and that often survives as checkerboard artefacts (Odena et al. 2016). Resizing (nearest or bilinear) followed by a regular convolution avoids it.
Whatever the method, upsampling increases sampling density; it cannot recover detail that the encoder never preserved. That is the job of skip connections.


14.5 Skip connections recover detail







Figure 59: Top: an early map \(C_2\) (stride 4) retains edges and exact positions; a deep map \(C_5\) (stride 32) encodes class and context, one cell per \(32\times32\) pixels. Bottom: the same FCN’s scores decoded with fine detail from stride 8 (boundaries follow the legs, the wheel, the dog) and from stride 32 only (blobs; the cyclist and the legs are lost).




Early maps retain edges, corners, and accurate coordinates; deep maps encode class and broad context. A skip connection carries an encoder map to the decoder stage of the same resolution, where it is concatenated with or added to the upsampled features, letting the decoder use both. The feature sizes must be aligned by padding, cropping, or resizing — this is where Equation 5 earns its keep.
Contrast this with ResNet: these links bridge scales, carrying fine detail to a coarse decoder; residual links mainly ease optimization within one scale.


14.6 U-Net







Figure 60: U-Net: a contracting path (pooling ÷2) and a symmetric expanding path (up-sampling ×2), with encoder maps copied and concatenated (cyan) to the decoder maps of the same resolution (orange). Activations from a ResNet encoder and an FCN’s prediction stand in for a trained U-Net.




U-Net (Ronneberger et al. 2015) was designed for biomedical images, where annotated data are scarce and boundaries matter. Its encoder and decoder are symmetric; skip features are concatenated, not merely added, so the decoder can learn how to combine them; and the result is strong localization with limited annotated data. The original network used unpadded convolutions (a \(572\times572\) input gives a \(388\times388\) output, with the copied maps cropped to match) and channel widths from 64 to 1024. Modern U-Nets add padding, normalization, and residual blocks — and U-Nets are also the denoising backbone of many diffusion models. The enduring idea: pair semantics with same-scale detail.


14.7 DeepLab: context at multiple scales







Figure 61: DeepLabV3 on the scene. Atrous spatial pyramid pooling runs, in parallel, a \(1\times1\) convolution, three \(3\times3\) atrous convolutions with rates 12, 24, and 36 at stride 8 (taps 96, 192, and 288 pixels apart; the paper’s rates 6, 12, 18 at stride 16 give the same spacing), and an image-pooling branch that averages the whole image; the branches are concatenated and projected to dense scores.




DeepLab takes the other route: instead of downsampling and recovering, it keeps the resolution higher (output stride 8 or 16) and enlarges the receptive field with atrous (dilated) convolutions:
\[
y[p]=\sum_{k}w[k]\,x[p+r k] .
\tag{18}\]
With rate \(r\), a \(3\times3\) kernel covers \((2r+1)\times(2r+1)\) pixels of its input with the same nine weights — a larger field of view without another pooling step, and without losing resolution. Atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASPP) runs several rates in parallel so that objects at different scales are captured, plus a global image-pooling branch for scene-level context (Chen et al. 2017). DeepLabV3+ adds a light decoder that fuses stride-4 features to sharpen boundaries (Chen et al. 2018). Multi-scale context disambiguates local texture using the surrounding scene: a grey patch is “road” because of what surrounds it.
from torchvision.models.segmentation import deeplabv3_resnet50, DeepLabV3_ResNet50_Weights

weights = DeepLabV3_ResNet50_Weights.DEFAULT        # 21 Pascal VOC classes
model = deeplabv3_resnet50(weights=weights).eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    logits = model(weights.transforms()(image).unsqueeze(0))["out"]  # (1, 21, H', W')
labels = logits.argmax(dim=1)                                        # (1, H', W')


14.8 Segmentation losses







Figure 62: A rare class. The dog covers \(5.5\%\) of the reference crop. DeepLabV3’s \(p(\text{dog})\) and its per-pixel cross-entropy, against a trivial model that predicts \(p=0.05\) everywhere: cross-entropy barely separates them (\(0.034\) against \(0.212\)), Dice does (\(0.21\) against \(0.95\)).




The default is pixel-wise cross-entropy, averaged over the set \(\Omega\) of labelled pixels, optionally with class weights \(w_c\):
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}=-\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_{i\in\Omega}\sum_{c=1}^{C}w_c\,y_{ic}\log p_{ic} .
\tag{19}\]
It is probabilistic and stable, and class weights can protect rare labels. Its weakness is that it is an average over pixels: thousands of easy background pixels can hide a badly segmented small object.
The soft Dice loss (Milletari et al. 2016) measures overlap directly, for one foreground class with predicted probabilities \(p_i\) and binary targets \(y_i\):
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}}=1-\frac{2\sum_i p_iy_i+\varepsilon}{\sum_i p_i+\sum_i y_i+\varepsilon} .
\tag{20}\]
It is a differentiable relaxation of the Dice coefficient \(2|A\cap B|/(|A|+|B|)\), and it sees the foreground region as a whole, which makes it useful for small foreground regions.

Worked example — Why cross-entropy hides the “always background” model
Predict \(p(\text{dog})=0.05\) at every pixel, when the dog covers a fraction \(f=0.055\) of the image. Per pixel, cross-entropy is \(-\ln0.05=3.00\) on dog pixels and \(-\ln0.95=0.051\) on background pixels, so \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}=0.055\cdot3.00+0.945\cdot0.051=0.165+0.048=0.212 .
\] For Dice, with \(n\) pixels, \(\sum_ip_iy_i=0.05\cdot0.055n\), \(\sum_ip_i=0.05n\), \(\sum_iy_i=0.055n\), and (ignoring \(\varepsilon\)) \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}}=1-\frac{2\cdot0.00275}{0.05+0.055}=1-0.052=0.95 .
\] The trivial model is only six times worse than DeepLabV3 under cross-entropy, but its Dice loss is near the maximum of \(1\).

A common recipe: start with cross-entropy; add Dice, focal, or boundary terms only for a diagnosed imbalance.
import torch.nn.functional as F

def soft_dice_loss(logits, target, eps=1.0):
    """logits: (B, H, W) for one foreground class; target: (B, H, W) in {0, 1}."""
    p = logits.sigmoid().flatten(1)
    t = target.float().flatten(1)
    dice = (2 * (p * t).sum(1) + eps) / (p.sum(1) + t.sum(1) + eps)
    return 1 - dice.mean()

# Multi-class cross-entropy on (B, C, H, W) logits and (B, H, W) labels;
# pixels labelled 255 (borders, "void") are excluded from the average.
ce = F.cross_entropy(logits, labels, ignore_index=255)


14.9 Segmentation metrics







Figure 63: For each class \(c\), over all pixels: true positives are pixels predicted \(c\) that are \(c\); false positives are extra pixels; false negatives are missed pixels.




\[
\text{pixel accuracy}=\frac{\sum_c\mathrm{TP}_c}{|\Omega|},
\qquad
\mathrm{IoU}_c=\frac{\mathrm{TP}_c}{\mathrm{TP}_c+\mathrm{FP}_c+\mathrm{FN}_c},
\qquad
\mathrm{mIoU}=\frac1C\sum_{c=1}^{C}\mathrm{IoU}_c .
\tag{21}\]
The counts are accumulated over the whole dataset before dividing, not averaged per image. Accuracy can look excellent when the background dominates; mIoU gives each class equal weight. And before comparing models, fix the ignore regions and the resize policy (is the metric computed at the original resolution or at the network’s?), which can move mIoU by several points.

Worked example — A model that predicts only “road”
Suppose road covers \(70\%\) of the pixels, cars \(20\%\), and people \(10\%\). A model that predicts “road” everywhere has pixel accuracy \(0.70\), which sounds respectable. But \(\mathrm{IoU}_{\text{road}}=0.70/(0.70+0.30+0)=0.70\), \(\mathrm{IoU}_{\text{car}}=\mathrm{IoU}_{\text{person}}=0\), so \(\mathrm{mIoU}=0.23\). The failure is invisible in accuracy and obvious in mIoU.

title: From pixels to structured scene understanding
text:
15 Instance and panoptic segmentation

15.1 Instance segmentation







Figure 64: Instance segmentation from Mask R-CNN: each countable object receives its own mask and identity — person 1, person 2, car 1, bus 1.




Instance segmentation predicts a set of object-level masks,
\[
\big\{(c_k,s_k,\mathbf{b}_k,\mathbf{M}_k)\big\}_{k=1}^{K},
\qquad
\mathbf{M}_k\in\{0,1\}^{H\times W},
\]
combining the set output of detection with the pixel accuracy of segmentation (Hariharan et al. 2014). Each countable thing receives an identity; overlapping objects remain separate; masks capture shape while boxes still help to localize the proposals. “Stuff” is usually left to a semantic branch. It is evaluated by mask AP: the AP of Section 8 with box IoU replaced by mask IoU.


15.2 Mask R-CNN







Figure 65: Mask R-CNN on the scene: backbone and FPN features (P2 shown, stride 4), RPN proposals (top 40 of about 1000), RoIAlign with \(7\times7\) bins and bilinear samples without rounding, the class and box head, and a parallel mask head — a small FCN — that predicts a \(28\times28\) mask per RoI, which is pasted back into its box.




Mask R-CNN (He et al. 2017) is Faster R-CNN with one extra branch. Faster R-CNN supplies proposals, classes, and boxes; a parallel FCN predicts an \(m\times m\) mask (\(m=28\)) for each RoI. Three design decisions matter.

RoIAlign instead of RoIPool. RoIPool rounds the proposal’s coordinates to the feature grid, then rounds again when dividing it into bins. At stride 16, a rounding of half a cell is 8 pixels — harmless for a box, ruinous for a boundary. RoIAlign keeps real-valued coordinates, samples each bin at regular points by bilinear interpolation, and averages: no quantization anywhere.
Per-class binary masks. The mask head outputs \(C\) masks of \(m\times m\) with a per-pixel sigmoid, and only the mask of the ground-truth class enters the loss — a pixel-wise binary cross-entropy. Classes do not compete inside the mask; the classification branch decides the class. This decoupling was found to work markedly better than a per-pixel softmax over classes.
Shared features. Detection and masks share the backbone, so the mask costs little extra.

Precise alignment matters when the output is a boundary, not just a box.


15.3 Panoptic segmentation
Semantic segmentation labels stuff and things but merges instances; instance segmentation separates things but ignores stuff. Panoptic segmentation (Kirillov et al. 2019) asks for both at once: every pixel gets a class and, for things, an instance identity, with no overlaps. It is evaluated with panoptic quality: predicted and ground-truth segments are matched when their IoU exceeds \(0.5\) (which makes the match unique), and
\[
\mathrm{PQ}=\frac{\sum_{(p,g)\in\mathrm{TP}}\operatorname{IoU}(p,g)}{|\mathrm{TP}|+\tfrac12|\mathrm{FP}|+\tfrac12|\mathrm{FN}|}
=\underbrace{\frac{\sum_{\mathrm{TP}}\operatorname{IoU}}{|\mathrm{TP}|}}_{\text{segmentation quality}}\times\underbrace{\frac{|\mathrm{TP}|}{|\mathrm{TP}|+\tfrac12|\mathrm{FP}|+\tfrac12|\mathrm{FN}|}}_{\text{recognition quality}},
\]
computed per class and averaged. PQ thus separates how well matched segments fit from how many segments were found.
Part VPose estimation and tracking

title: From pixels to structured scene understanding
text:
16 Human pose estimation







Figure 66: 2D keypoints and anatomical links on the scene.




Pose estimation predicts a structured set of landmarks for a person (or an animal, a hand, an object):
\[
\mathcal{K}=\{(x_j,y_j,v_j)\}_{j=1}^{J},
\]
where \(v_j\) records visibility or confidence. COCO uses \(J=17\) body keypoints (nose, eyes, ears, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles) with \(v_j\in\{0,1,2\}\) for “not labelled”, “labelled but occluded”, and “visible”.

2D or 3D. 2D pose gives keypoints in image coordinates; 3D pose gives joints in camera or world coordinates — an ill-posed lifting problem in the sense of Equation 1.
Structure. A fixed skeleton graph connects related joints; predictions that violate it (a wrist far from its elbow) are implausible.
Multiple people add a second problem: assigning joints to identities.

The first deep approach, DeepPose (Toshev and Szegedy 2014), regressed the \(2J\) coordinates directly with a CNN. Almost all later methods predict heatmaps instead (Section 16.3), and differ in how they handle multiple people.

16.1 Top-down pose estimation







Figure 67: Top-down pose estimation with Keypoint R-CNN on the scene. A person detector finds \(N=3\) people of any size; each is cropped and resized to \(192\times256\) pixels with one person centred; a single-person network predicts 17 keypoints per crop; the keypoints are mapped back to the image.




Detect first, then estimate one pose per detection (Xiao et al. 2018). Each crop is mapped back to the image by undoing the crop and the resize,
\[
(x,y)_{\text{image}}=\text{box corner}+\text{scale}\cdot(x,y)_{\text{crop}} .
\]
Why it works well: each crop has normalized scale, little background, and one main subject, so a high-resolution head can refine joint locations. The detector is the bottleneck: a missed or badly cropped person cannot be recovered, and the runtime grows roughly with the number of people detected. Top-down methods trade detector dependence and per-person cost for clean single-person reasoning.


16.2 Bottom-up pose estimation







Figure 68: Bottom-up pose estimation. One pass over the whole image detects all joint candidates — their type is known, their owner is not; a pairwise limb-affinity score is computed for candidate pairs (here the \(2\times2\) left-hip–left-knee pairs, drawn schematically); matched limbs are chained into person 1 and person 2.




Detect all body parts first, then solve identity through grouping. OpenPose (Cao et al. 2017) computes keypoint heatmaps once for the whole scene, plus part affinity fields — 2D vector fields along each limb whose line integral between two candidate joints scores how likely they belong to one limb — and then assembles compatible limbs into people by a greedy matching on the skeleton tree.
The trade-offs mirror the top-down ones: the cost depends only weakly on crowd size; small people must share the same feature-map resolution as large ones; and grouping becomes ambiguous under overlap and occlusion.


16.3 Heatmap regression







Figure 69: Real Keypoint R-CNN heatmaps (log scale, \(56\times56\) cells over the person box) for 4 of the 17 joints; the knee and the ankle show a weaker second peak on the other leg. Bottom: a \(9\times9\)-cell zoom (1 cell \(=2.2\) pixels) of a Gaussian target (\(\sigma=1.5\) cells) and of the prediction, with the decoded sub-cell keypoint.




Instead of regressing \((x_j,y_j)\), predict one map per joint and train it towards a Gaussian bump centred at the target position \(\mathbf{p}_j\) (Newell et al. 2016):
\[
H_j(\mathbf{p})=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{p}_j\rVert_2^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right),
\qquad
\hat{\mathbf{p}}_j=\arg\max_{\mathbf{p}}\hat H_j(\mathbf{p}).
\tag{22}\]

Train with mean-squared error between \(\hat H_j\) and \(H_j\), or with a normalized spatial loss. Heatmaps preserve uncertainty better than direct regression, and they keep the output spatially aligned with the convolutional features — the same reason dense prediction works.
Heatmaps live on a downsampled grid (typically stride 4), so the arg max is quantized to a cell. Refinement — shifting a quarter of a cell towards the second-highest neighbour — or a soft-argmax, \(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_j=\sum_{\mathbf{p}}\mathbf{p}\,\operatorname{softmax}(\beta\hat H_j)(\mathbf{p})\), restores sub-pixel precision; the soft-argmax is also differentiable.
Multiple peaks can represent ambiguity (which knee is the left one?) or multiple people in the crop.



16.4 Pose metrics
PCK (percentage of correct keypoints): a joint is correct when \(\lVert\hat{\mathbf{p}}_j-\mathbf{p}_j\rVert_2\le\alpha L\), where \(L\) is a person, torso, or head scale; average the indicator over joints. PCKh@0.5 (Andriluka et al. 2014) uses \(\alpha=0.5\) and the head-segment length.
Object keypoint similarity plays for poses the role IoU plays for boxes. With \(\mathcal{V}=\{j:v_j>0\}\) the labelled keypoints,
\[
\mathrm{OKS}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{V}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{d_j^{2}}{2s^{2}\kappa_j^{2}}\right),
\tag{23}\]
where \(d_j\) is the keypoint error, \(s\) the person scale (\(s^2\) is the object’s segment area in COCO), and \(\kappa_j\) a per-keypoint tolerance — larger for hips, whose position is ambiguous even to annotators, than for eyes. Keypoint AP treats OKS like IoU: match poses at several OKS thresholds, build precision–recall curves, and average; COCO reports AP@[.50:.95]. Compare pose scores only under the same scale, visibility, matching, and threshold protocol.


16.5 Applications and failure modes







Figure 70: Occlusion by the pole and the dog leash makes some keypoints low-confidence.




Pose estimation serves sports analysis, human–robot interaction, ergonomics, animation and augmented reality, rehabilitation, and gesture interfaces. It fails under occlusion, truncation, and crowded overlap; rare viewpoints and unusual articulation; blur, low resolution, or loose clothing; left/right swaps and implausible limbs; and domain and demographic shift (Ronchi and Perona 2017).

title: From pixels to structured scene understanding
text:
17 Multi-object tracking







Figure 71: Multi-object tracking: the same identities — ID 3, ID 7, ID 9 — followed from the past to the present.




Given detections over a video, multi-object tracking (MOT) estimates trajectories
\[
\mathcal{T}_i=\big\{(t,\mathbf{b}^{i}_t,c_i,\mathrm{ID}_i)\big\}_{t=t_s}^{t_e}.
\]
The task has four parts: localize each object at each time; preserve a stable identity through motion and occlusion; start and terminate tracks as objects enter or leave; and diagnose false and missed tracks, fragmentation, and identity switches (Milan et al. 2016).

17.1 Tracking by detection







Figure 72: One step of tracking by detection on the scene. (1) Detect at frame \(t\) (white boxes). (2) Predict each track forward from \(t-1\) (dashed; frame \(t-1\) is simulated). (3) Gate and build the cost matrix \(c_{ij}=1-\operatorname{IoU}(\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i,\mathbf{d}_j)\), with pairs of IoU below \(0.3\) gated out (×). (4) Solve a minimum-cost one-to-one assignment: \(T_5\), hidden behind the pole, and \(d_5\), the dog, stay unmatched. (5) Update: matched tracks are corrected by their detection; the unmatched detection starts a tentative new track; the unmatched track is kept briefly and deleted after repeated misses.




The dominant paradigm runs a detector on every frame and links detections over time. SORT (Bewley et al. 2016) is the minimal, and surprisingly strong, version:

Detect objects in frame \(t\): \(\{\mathbf{d}_j\}\).
Predict every existing track forward with a motion model: \(\{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i\}\).
Gate and build a cost matrix \(\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times D}\); implausible pairs get infinite cost.
Assign one-to-one by the Hungarian algorithm — the same tool as DETR’s matching.
Update each track’s state and lifecycle.

A simple online loop becomes a tracker when association and lifecycle rules are explicit. Lifecycle rules matter as much as the cost: a new detection starts a tentative track that is confirmed after a few consecutive matches (three in Deep SORT); a confirmed track that goes unmatched is kept alive for a number of frames (up to 30 in Deep SORT), so that it can survive a short occlusion, then deleted.


17.2 Motion: the Kalman filter
SORT models each box with a constant-velocity Kalman filter whose state is the box centre, its scale (area), and its aspect ratio, plus the velocities of the first three: \(\mathbf{x}=[u,v,s,r,\dot u,\dot v,\dot s]^\top\). The model is linear-Gaussian,
\[
\mathbf{x}_t=\mathbf{F}\mathbf{x}_{t-1}+\mathbf{w}_t,
\quad\mathbf{w}_t\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{Q}),
\qquad
\mathbf{z}_t=\mathbf{H}\mathbf{x}_t+\mathbf{n}_t,
\quad\mathbf{n}_t\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{R}),
\]
where \(\mathbf{F}\) adds each velocity to its position and \(\mathbf{H}\) picks the observed box \((u,v,s,r)\) out of the state. Each frame alternates two steps.
\[
\textbf{Predict:}\quad
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t|t-1}=\mathbf{F}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t-1|t-1},
\qquad
\mathbf{P}_{t|t-1}=\mathbf{F}\mathbf{P}_{t-1|t-1}\mathbf{F}^\top+\mathbf{Q}.
\]
\[
\textbf{Update:}\quad
\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{H}\mathbf{P}_{t|t-1}\mathbf{H}^\top+\mathbf{R},
\quad
\mathbf{K}=\mathbf{P}_{t|t-1}\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{S}^{-1},
\quad
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t|t}=\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t|t-1}+\mathbf{K}\big(\mathbf{z}_t-\mathbf{H}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t|t-1}\big),
\quad
\mathbf{P}_{t|t}=(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{K}\mathbf{H})\mathbf{P}_{t|t-1}.
\]
The prediction moves the box and grows its uncertainty \(\mathbf{P}\); the update pulls it towards the matched detection, weighted by the Kalman gain \(\mathbf{K}\), and shrinks the uncertainty. An unmatched track only predicts, so its uncertainty keeps growing during an occlusion.
The innovation covariance \(\mathbf{S}\) gives a principled gate: the squared Mahalanobis distance \(d^2=(\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{H}\hat{\mathbf{x}})^\top\mathbf{S}^{-1}(\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{H}\hat{\mathbf{x}})\) follows a \(\chi^2\) distribution if the detection belongs to the track, so pairs with \(d^2\) above the \(95\%\) quantile — \(5.99\) for a 2-D position, \(9.49\) for a 4-D box — are rejected.


17.3 Motion, geometry, and appearance for association







Figure 73: Combining cues for tracks \(T_3\) (cyclist) and \(T_4\) (woman) against detections \(d_3\), \(d_4\), \(d_5\). Motion: the ellipse is the gate around the Kalman prediction; pairs outside it (\(d^2>5.99\)) are never matched. Geometry: \(1-\mathrm{IoU}\) between the predicted and detected boxes. Appearance: \(1-\cos\) of ResNet-18 embeddings of the crops. With \(C=0.5\,\text{geo}+0.5\,\text{app}\), the Hungarian matches are \(T_3\to d_3\) (\(C=0.10\)) and \(T_4\to d_4\) (\(C=0.11\)); the woman and the dog are far apart in appearance (\(0.53\)).




For track \(i\) and detection \(j\), combine a geometric and an appearance cost on the pairs that pass the gate:
\[
c^{\text{geo}}_{ij}=1-\operatorname{IoU}(\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i,\mathbf{d}_j),
\qquad
c^{\text{app}}_{ij}=1-\mathbf{e}_i^\top\mathbf{e}_j,
\qquad
C_{ij}=\lambda_g c^{\text{geo}}_{ij}+\lambda_a c^{\text{app}}_{ij},
\qquad
\pi^{*}=\arg\min_{\pi}\sum_iC_{i,\pi(i)},
\tag{24}\]
where \(\mathbf{e}\) are L2-normalized appearance embeddings — in Deep SORT (Wojke et al. 2017), from a network trained for person re-identification, and for each track, the best match over a gallery of its recent appearances. Each cue covers a different failure: motion rejects implausible jumps; IoU favours spatial continuity between consecutive frames; appearance recovers identities after crossings and short occlusions, when the motion prediction has drifted.
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment
from torchvision.ops import box_iou

def associate(pred_boxes, det_boxes, iou_min=0.3):
    """pred_boxes: (T, 4) Kalman predictions; det_boxes: (D, 4). Returns matched pairs."""
    cost = 1 - box_iou(pred_boxes, det_boxes).numpy()
    cost[cost > 1 - iou_min] = 1e6                     # gate implausible pairs
    rows, cols = linear_sum_assignment(cost)
    return [(r, c) for r, c in zip(rows, cols) if cost[r, c] < 1e6]


17.4 Tracking metrics
The taxonomy table listed HOTA and IDF1. Three metrics are in common use, and they weigh errors differently.

MOTA (Bernardin and Stiefelhagen 2008) counts the three error types per frame: \(\mathrm{MOTA}=1-\frac{\sum_t(\mathrm{FN}_t+\mathrm{FP}_t+\mathrm{IDSW}_t)}{\sum_t\mathrm{GT}_t}\). Because detection errors vastly outnumber identity switches, MOTA is dominated by detection quality.
IDF1 (Ristani et al. 2016) first matches whole predicted trajectories to whole ground-truth trajectories, then computes an F1 score of correctly identified detections: \(\mathrm{IDF1}=\frac{2\,\mathrm{IDTP}}{2\,\mathrm{IDTP}+\mathrm{IDFP}+\mathrm{IDFN}}\). It emphasizes keeping identities over time.
HOTA (Luiten et al. 2021) balances the two explicitly: at a localization threshold \(\alpha\), \(\mathrm{HOTA}_\alpha=\sqrt{\mathrm{DetA}_\alpha\cdot\mathrm{AssA}_\alpha}\), the geometric mean of a detection accuracy and an association accuracy, then averages over \(\alpha\in\{0.05,0.10,\dots,0.95\}\).

Report more than one, and say which: a tracker can improve MOTA by detecting more while switching identities more often.

title: From pixels to structured scene understanding
text:
18 Exercises

18.1 Exercise 1 — Shape arithmetic
A \(224\times224\times3\) image passes through: a \(7\times7\) convolution with 64 filters, stride 2, padding 3; a \(3\times3\) max pool, stride 2, padding 1; and two \(3\times3\) convolutions with 64 filters, stride 1, padding 1. Give the output shape after each layer and the parameter count of each convolution (with biases). Then compute the receptive field and the jump of the last layer with Equation 6.


18.2 Exercise 2 — Equivariance and its limits
Show that a stride-1 convolution with circular padding is exactly equivariant to circular shifts. Then give a 1-D example where a convolution with stride 2 is not equivariant to a shift by one sample. What does this imply for the robustness of a CNN classifier to one-pixel shifts?


18.3 Exercise 3 — ViT budget
For ViT-B/16 (\(D=768\), \(L=12\), \(h=12\)), compute \(N\), the number of multiply–adds of the attention matrices (\(2N^2D\)) and of the linear layers (\(12ND^2\)) per block, for \(224\times224\) and for \(1024\times1024\) inputs. At which resolution do they become equal? Repeat with patch size 8. Which design changes would you consider for dense prediction at \(1024\times1024\)?


18.4 Exercise 4 — IoU and anchors
Compute the IoU of the boxes \((0,0,4,4)\) and \((2,2,6,6)\), and their GIoU. Then encode the ground truth \((100,100,200,150)\) (corner form) against the anchor \((c_x,c_y,w,h)=(140,130,128,64)\) with Equation 14, and decode it back.


18.5 Exercise 5 — Average precision by hand
A detector returns, for one class, predictions with scores \(0.95, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5\) whose matching outcomes are TP, TP, FP, TP, FP, TP, on a dataset with 5 ground-truth objects. Trace the precision–recall points, interpolate, and compute AP with the all-point method. What is the maximum recall, and why is it not 1?


18.6 Exercise 6 — Focal loss gradients
Differentiate \(\operatorname{FL}(p_t)\) with respect to the logit \(x\) of a positive anchor (\(p_t=\sigma(x)\)), and plot the gradient magnitude against \(p_t\) for \(\gamma\in\{0,1,2,5\}\). Explain in one paragraph why the shares in Figure 45 move as they do.


18.7 Exercise 7 — NMS versus set prediction
Implement greedy NMS in fewer than fifteen lines of PyTorch and check it against torchvision.ops.nms. Construct a case with two heavily overlapping objects of the same class where NMS must fail at any threshold, and explain why a DETR-style set predictor does not have this failure in principle.


18.8 Exercise 8 — Segmentation losses and metrics
For a \(10\times10\) binary image with a \(2\times2\) foreground square, compute pixel accuracy, foreground IoU, mIoU (two classes), cross-entropy, and Dice loss for (a) a prediction of \(p=0.1\) everywhere and (b) a prediction that is correct except for a one-pixel shift of the square. Which metric and which loss rank the two predictions as you would?


18.9 Exercise 9 — A tracker in practice (preparation for TP 1)
Run torchvision’s Faster R-CNN on every frame of a short video. Implement the association of Equation 24 with IoU only, then add a constant-velocity Kalman filter and gating, then an appearance term using a pretrained ResNet-18 embedding of each crop. Count identity switches by inspection for each version, and relate each improvement to the failure it addresses.

title: From pixels to structured scene understanding
text:
19 Main takeaways

Match the output to the task. Classification predicts labels; detection, sets of boxes; segmentation, labels for pixels; pose, keypoints; tracking, identities through time. The output space determines the annotation, the head, the loss, the inference procedure, and the metric.
Learn useful representations. CNNs encode locality and translation structure and are data-efficient; ViTs use content-dependent global interaction and need more data or pretraining. Both serve as reusable backbones, and hierarchical models such as Swin and feature pyramids give the multi-scale maps dense tasks need.
Share computation. The step from sliding windows to fully convolutional networks — run the backbone once, predict everywhere — underlies detection, segmentation, and bottom-up pose alike.
Assignment defines learning. Anchor matching, Hungarian matching in DETR, and data association in tracking all decide which prediction is responsible for which target; the losses are only computed afterwards.
Resolution versus context is the central tension of dense prediction. Skip connections, atrous convolutions, feature pyramids, RoIAlign, and heatmap refinement are all answers to it.
Evaluate what matters. Use task-aligned metrics (AP over IoU thresholds, mIoU, OKS AP, HOTA and IDF1) under a fixed protocol, and slice errors by scale, class, occlusion, localization, and identity.
Build by diagnosing failures. Start with a measurable baseline, visualize its mistakes, and add complexity only to address a specific failure. Align representation, output, loss, metric, and data with the failure you need to fix.

This web note is adapted from the Lecture 1 slides of Deep Learning for Computer Vision by Jhony H. Giraldo. The course logistics were moved to the course page; the derivations, worked examples, code, and exercises were expanded; and several topics that the slides only name were developed: COCO-style AP, GIoU, Swin’s attention cost, the Kalman filter, panoptic quality, and the MOTA, IDF1, and HOTA metrics.
The figures are cropped from the compiled slides by scripts/figures/dl4cv_lecture_01_figures.py in this repository. Most of them are original TikZ drawn over a street scene generated for the lecture with an image-generation model, annotated with the outputs of torchvision’s pretrained models (BSD-3-Clause). Where no model was available, the slides use labelled stand-ins: Faster R-CNN’s confident detections as “ground truth”, RetinaNet boxes in place of DETR outputs, ResNet and FCN maps in place of a trained U-Net, schematic limb affinities for bottom-up pose, and a simulated frame \(t-1\) for tracking. The slides’ CPU timings (29.4 s and 0.58 s) were measured on the machine that generated the figures.
